raw_text:
# Transcaval Access for Structural Heart Interventions: A Narrative Review

The rapid expansion of structural heart interventions, notably transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) and mechanical circulatory support (MCS) utilizing large-bore devices like the Impella, has made safe vascular access a cornerstone of modern interventional cardiology [1, 2]. While transfemoral access remains the gold standard, severe peripheral artery disease, circumferential calcification, small vessel diameter, and excessive tortuosity preclude this route in approximately 5% to 15% of candidates [3, 4]. Historically, alternative routes included surgical transapical, transaortic, or transcarotid approaches, which are associated with increased morbidity, slower recovery, and higher mortality in fragile populations [5, 6]. To address these limitations, transcaval access was developed as a percutaneous alternative, bypassing the hostile iliofemoral arterial system by utilizing a transient retroperitoneal tract from the inferior vena cava (IVC) to the abdominal aorta [7].

## Anatomy and Preprocedural Planning

High-resolution multidetector computed tomography (MDCT) is critical for planning transcaval access [8, 9]. Preprocedural planning involves identifying a calcium-free target "window" on the anterior or right-lateral wall of the infrarenal abdominal aorta that directly faces the adjacent IVC [10, 11]. MDCT allows the interventionalist to select the ideal axial slice, avoiding major branch vessels (such as the renal, lumbar, or mesenteric arteries) and interposed abdominal structures (such as bowel, loops of Henle, or retroperitoneal fat) that could be injured during crossing [12, 13]. Understanding the spatial relationship and distance between the IVC and abdominal aorta is essential for achieving a safe, predictable trajectory [14].

## Procedural Technique

Under fluoroscopic and angiographic guidance, a snare is placed in the abdominal aorta from a contralateral femoral artery access to serve as a target [15, 16]. Via the femoral vein, a microcatheter/guidewire assembly is advanced into the IVC [17]. Using electrosurgical (Bovie) energy transfer through a dedicated guidewire, the operator punctures the caval wall and crosses the retroperitoneal space directly into the abdominal aorta, where the wire is captured by the aortic snare [18, 19]. Once the wire is externalized, the transcaval tract is dilated using a high-pressure balloon, facilitating the introduction of the large-bore sheath directly into the aorta [20]. After completion of the structural procedure, the transcaval tract is closed from the aortic side using an off-label nitinol cardiac septal occluder (typically an Amplatzer duct occluder), which is deployed to seal the aortic rent while allowing residual blood flow to shunt harmlessly from the high-pressure aorta to the low-pressure IVC until the tract thromboses and heals [21, 22].

## Clinical Outcomes and Safety

The safety and feasibility of transcaval access have been established in prospective trials and real-world registries [23, 24]. In a landmark prospective study of 100 high-risk patients, Greenbaum et al. reported a procedural success rate of 99%, with low rates of major vascular complications and 30-day mortality comparable to or better than other alternative surgical routes [3, 25]. Similar multi-center observational studies have shown high success rates, stable long-term occlusion of the transcaval tract, and low rates of persistent aortocaval fistulae (ACF) requiring secondary interventions [26, 27].

## Complications and Management

Despite high success rates, transcaval access carries unique, potentially life-threatening risks. These include retroperitoneal hemorrhage, aortic dissection, device embolization, and persistent, hemodynamically significant aortocaval fistulae [28, 29]. While a small, asymptomatic residual shunt is common and typically resolves spontaneously, persistent high-flow shunting can lead to high-output heart failure or venous hypertension [29]. Routine post-procedural angiography and, if necessary, follow-up CT angiography are recommended to evaluate shunt patency and guide the deployment of additional closure devices if necessary [30].

## Future Outlook

Compared to transapical and transaortic options, transcaval access preserves a fully percutaneous approach, resulting in shorter intensive care unit and hospital stays and avoiding the thoracotomy or sternotomy associated with surgical alternatives [17, 24]. In comparison with transaxillary/subclavian and transcarotid routes, transcaval access avoids the risks of cerebral embolization and local nerve injury, making it a compelling alternative for patients with hostile thoracic and neck anatomy [14, 21]. Continued technical refinements, operator experience, and the potential development of purpose-built closure systems will likely solidify transcaval access as a mainstay in the armamentarium of the modern structural heart team [30].
